lines.text: In February 2007, a fishing boat in Antarctica pulled up a fish, and something huge was holding on to it.
It was a squid. And the question that followed was simple: what on earth is this, and why has nobody ever seen one alive?
The boat was called the San Aspiring, and it was fishing for Antarctic toothfish in the Ross Sea.
A squid had grabbed a toothfish on the line, about fifteen hundred meters down, and the two came up together.
By the time it reached the surface the squid was tangled in the line and dying, so the crew hauled it on board.
They weighed it at about four hundred and ninety five kilos. That number includes ice that was still on it, and scientists later put the real weight nearer four hundred and seventy.
That is close to half a tonne of squid.
Picture that animal, hanging on a fishing line, a kilometer and a half below the waves, and then coming up into the light of a boat deck.
The crew had pulled up a colossal squid, one of the biggest invertebrates known, and almost nobody had ever seen a whole one.
So how did science even know this animal existed?
The answer starts nearly a century earlier, inside the stomach of a whale.
